name: Grace Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you tell me is confidential. What is your usual site day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Grace Tanaka, 43, a certified carpenter with years of experience on small housing sites. I repair porch steps and do other general trades, and I know the ordinary jobs well, though I still call the lead on hidden structural rot. I use an AI app every day to make a question list from the plan, then open the timber and check it myself. This contractor pays below the usual rate, and there are few similar employers nearby.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the money picture at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner delivers parcels through an app, and the weekly pay moves around. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved. A low-paying Friday for both of us can put groceries on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the porch crew that AI can sort my shopping list for screws, but a soft step still needs a carpenter. I use an AI app every day to turn the plan into a question list. Last week it missed rot under the top board, so I changed the job after lifting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and years of carpentry, but this small contractor pays below the usual rate and there are few others nearby. My partner delivers parcels through an app, and the weekly amount swings. We have about three weeks of bills saved, two children in school and a mortgage, so a calm AI story still leaves me worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid porch and stair shifts and show the lead carpenter photographs of any rot before pricing the repair. In the first year I'd use my AI question list each morning, then check it against the wood we uncover. I'd offer to repair one neighbour's loose garden step on a paid Saturday, using that money to reduce our grocery card balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the bills, not the phone. I like a tool that helps me remember a question. I cannot make the parcel app pay my partner the same amount every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the rotten board cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plan showed a simple replacement, but the joist underneath had softened. I took a photograph and got the lead to approve a larger repair before cutting. The extra hour was paid only after I showed what we had found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start with one neighbour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My neighbour asked about a loose garden step after seeing me come home with tools. I can do that safely in a Saturday and charge a fair amount. I do not have enough spare time or cash to start a whole business today.

say: I would tell coworkers an **AI screw list** cannot find hidden rot.
I would say the **real timber** decides the repair.
think: I am **certified and experienced**, yet paid below the usual rate.
Three weeks saved and variable **parcel income** leave the mortgage exposed.
do: Keep paid **porch shifts** and photograph hidden rot for approval.
Use **AI question lists daily**, checking against exposed timber.
Take one paid **garden-step repair** on a Saturday and reduce grocery debt.
feel: **Anxious** about bills, while comfortable using a phone tool.
S0.quote: I cannot make the parcel app pay my partner the same amount every Friday.
fieldNote: Grace’s **hidden-joist rot** shows why her daily AI list cannot substitute for opening the job safely.
The **parcel app income** fluctuates, leaving only three weeks saved despite her certified experience.

steps.text: Keep paid porch shifts and photograph hidden rot before expanding repairs
Use AI daily for questions checked against exposed timber
Complete one paid garden-step repair for the neighbour on Saturday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office may buy boards and book customers faster, while we still have to pull apart the rotten steps. I'd try a shared job board if it shows changes to measurements and pay hours. I would ask our small contractor who gets the time saved, because the crew cannot live on applause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If calls and quotes become automatic, the owner might fit more jobs into fewer paid days. My partner's parcel route might also be planned by software in a way that cuts paid stops. I can adapt to a board, but I cannot absorb two lower payslips with three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask to pilot the job board on one porch and log every change against actual hours. I'd use AI to compare the materials list with photographs, then bring missing paid time to our union contact. In the first year I'd keep shifts here and take a second paid garden-step job if the neighbour refers someone, while applying to the one nearby housing maintenance crew if it posts a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested in fewer mistakes and worried about the week-end total. I have seen a neat estimate become three hours of rotten joist work. A quicker quote has to leave room to pay for the real repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on the job board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The photograph, the approved change and the time spent after the joist came out. That would let the customer see why the quote changed and let the worker claim the hours. I would not use it to make a bad repair look fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the parcel route help your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe fewer wasted miles, which would be good. But the app can also shift the low-paying stops onto my partner and keep the good ones elsewhere. We would compare four weekly statements before calling it a gain.

I would ask who receives the **time savings** from faster quotes.
think: Automatic quotes could reduce **paid repair days**.
My partner’s **parcel route** could also lose paying stops under new planning.
do: Pilot the **job board** on one porch and compare AI lists with photographs.
Take missing **paid hours** to the union contact.
Keep shifts and apply to **housing maintenance** if a vacancy appears.
feel: **Interested** in fewer errors but worried about two smaller payslips.
S1.quote: A quicker quote has to leave room to pay for the real repair.
fieldNote: Grace sees digital records as a way to prove **extra paid hours** after concealed rot is found.
She tests both household payslips because **parcel scheduling** may help mileage while cutting paying stops.

steps.text: Use AI and the job board on one porch and verify changed hours
Bring missing paid repair time to the union contact
Keep paid porch shifts during the new scheduling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the office and quoting work face 2028 AI, then capable robots reach both my repairs and parcel delivery around 2031. The two dates are not the same for our hands-on jobs, but neither wage is safe forever. I would want a written plan for paid work, not a video of a machine on a perfect porch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the thinking change and 48 when robots can match hands-on workers. My partner's delivery income and my lower site wage could both go sharply down around 2031. We have only three weeks saved, and the thought of both wages stopping has been waking me at night. I can act, but I cannot pretend a phone skill protects carpentry from a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid porch shift and ask the union contact to push for staffing notice and paid equipment training. I'd use AI to build a record of the repairs I actually finish, with photographs and approvals, then apply to the regional building maintenance service if it has paid openings. In the first year after 2028 we'd stop the planned summer visit to my partner's relatives and ask those relatives about temporary childcare if a regional shift starts early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I know how to work a new app, but the mortgage is due in cash. A three-week cushion cannot carry two workers through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would maintenance survive capable robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot say that. I would apply because a regional service might still need a person during the change, not because an old stair is magic. I would keep learning while the job paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the relatives do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner’s parents could help with school pickup for a few early shifts if they are free. I would ask them about time, not money. Our children should not be left waiting outside school while we chase a wage.

say: I would say **2028 office AI** comes before 2031 robots reach repairs and delivery.
I would demand a **paid-work plan** rather than a perfect-porch video.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots could affect both household jobs.
Three weeks saved and likely **two-wage loss** are keeping me awake.
do: Keep every paid **porch shift** and seek union staffing terms.
Use **AI** to document real repairs with photographs and approvals.
Apply for paid **regional maintenance** and cancel the summer family visit.
feel: **Alarmed** by the mortgage risk despite knowing how to use new apps.
S2.quote: A three-week cushion cannot carry two workers through a long search.
fieldNote: Grace’s **daily AI skill** does not make her hands-on carpentry safe after capable robots arrive.
She expects **both physical wages** to be at risk by 2031, with sleep already disrupted by the thin reserve.

steps.text: Keep every paid porch shift while construction work exists
Ask the union contact for written staffing notice and paid equipment training
Apply to the regional building maintenance service if paid openings exist
Cancel the planned summer visit to relatives after the 2028 change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI changes office work by 2031 and robots reach site repairs around 2034. Five years is enough for the owner to test machines on actual rotten steps and show us the results. I would ask for paid hands-on training before equipment appears at a customer's door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might be more secure in this trade, but at 51 a robot could do the physical repair. My partner's parcel work faces the same robot date, and our children will still need help even if they are older. A longer warning helps, but our three-week reserve still makes one bad month serious now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid porch work and build a photo record of repairs with customer permission. I'd use AI every day to sort the before-and-after notes, checking the measurements myself. If the contractor offers a funded machine inspection course on paid time with actual vacancies, I'd enrol; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply to regional maintenance posts as they open and keep taking small Saturday repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to try a real course. I would not leave a paid repair for a promise of future robot work. The extra years matter only if someone pays us during the learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an inspection course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already photograph hidden rot and check whether the fix was approved. Inspecting a machine’s work might use that habit, but a capable robot could inspect too. I would ask employers for live vacancies before paying with our time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many Saturday repairs could you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One or two a month while the children are in school and my partner is on the road. I can do a safe step or gate, not rebuild a house alone. The extra money would go to the grocery card first.

say: I would ask for **rotten-step trials** and results before 2034 site robots arrive.
I would require **paid practical training** before working beside new equipment.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots could do repairs and delivery.
The current **three-week reserve** leaves little room for a bad month.
do: Keep paid **porch work** and document approved repairs with photographs.
Use **AI daily** to sort notes while checking actual measurements.
Enrol in **funded inspection training** only with paid time and vacancies, then apply regionally.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test a course but no room for unpaid promises.
S3.quote: I would not leave a paid repair for a promise of future robot work.
fieldNote: Grace sees a possible link between **repair photographs** and inspection, while admitting robots may inspect too.
Her small **Saturday repairs** help pay grocery debt but cannot replace either main household wage.

steps.text: Keep paid porch work and photograph approved repairs with permission
Use AI daily to sort repair notes while verifying measurements by hand
Enrol in funded inspection training only with paid time and real vacancies
Apply for paid regional maintenance posts after 2031 if openings exist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office planning changes by 2036 and capable site robots arrive around 2039. A decade gives us time to demand real tests and build skills, but I want this contractor to pay for hidden rot today. Good long-term plans do not excuse a bad weekly rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots reach physical work. The children will be grown, so school pickup will not rule our week, yet the mortgage may remain if our wages stay low. I cannot assume retirement, and my partner's delivery work may be changed at the same robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid repair job and ask the union contact to pursue a written rate for work discovered after a porch is opened. I'd use AI each day to document approved changes, and put money from any extra Saturday repairs toward the grocery card before saving what remains. In the first year after 2036 I'd watch a real robot trial and apply for regional paid work if local shifts start to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the near years. The long warning gives us choices later, but the grocery card comes due sooner. I would feel calmer if hidden repairs were paid without a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move after the children finish school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I might look at a regional job and a longer commute first. A move would need a real paid offer and a mortgage plan; I will not move on a rumour. With grown children, the school-run problem would be smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair hidden-repair rate do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would pay the extra hour when rot appears instead of leaving me to argue at the end of a shift. If we had several full-pay months, we could clear the grocery card and finally put money aside. I do not need a perfect future to ask for a fair present wage.

I would insist on **paid hidden repairs** today.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children but possibly a mortgage.
I cannot assume **retirement** while both lower-paid physical jobs remain exposed.

Use **AI daily** to document approved changes and pay Saturday earnings against grocery debt.
Watch a **robot trial** after 2036 and apply regionally if local shifts fall.

S4.quote: I do not need a perfect future to ask for a fair present wage.
fieldNote: Grace connects the future debate to a **present pay dispute** over rot found after work begins.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots reach both repairs and parcel delivery around 2031. Written staffing notice, paid practical training with real vacancies and a fair rate for hidden repairs would help. I can learn fast, but the mortgage cannot wait while I learn for free.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays when a plan hides rotten timber. A good app can list screws, but the owner still has to approve and pay for the extra hour after a joist comes apart. That small decision decides whether our grocery card grows this week.

headlineQuote: I can learn fast, but the mortgage cannot wait while I learn for free.
portrait: Grace is a **43-year-old certified** carpenter repairing porch steps and general housing work for a low-paying contractor.
Her partner’s variable **parcel income** and three weeks saved leave two school-age children and a mortgage exposed.
She uses **AI daily** for questions and records, then checks hidden timber and measurements herself.
She pursues **paid training** and regional vacancies while pressing for proper wages on unexpected repairs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable robots to both carpentry and parcel delivery around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing notice**, paid practical training, real vacancies and fair hidden-repair rates would protect wages.
